justification: The paper never clarifies whether the hash grid is built once prior to training or reconstructed during training.

claim: The authors do not analyze reasons why their method outperforms transformer-based methods despite being an efficient simplification of PointNet++.
justification: The paper provides empirical comparisons but no specific analysis explaining why it outperforms transformer-based methods despite its PointNet++ simplification.

claim: There is a possible notation error where x_i might actually be p_i in Line 101.
justification: The paper provides no mention of Line 101 or any notation error confusing x_i with p_i, so the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: There is a significant gap between the paper's theoretical analysis and the experimental settings used in the evaluations.
justification: The paper does not discuss any gap between its theoretical analysis and the experimental settings, leaving the claim unsupported by the text.

claim: Theorem 4.1's stationary points may not correspond to generalized Nash equilibria, calling the theoretical guarantees into question.
justification: Theorem 4.1 only guarantees convergence to stationary points of exploitability, not zero exploitability, so those points need not be generalized Nash equilibria.

claim: The paper frequently claims the method maps pseudo-games to GNE without providing clear theoretical justification for that mapping.
justification: The paper provides formal theoretical justification for mapping pseudo-games to GNE via Observation 1 and convergence/sample complexity proofs in Theorems 4.1 and 4.2.

claim: Theorem 4.1 assumes strong concavity, an assumption that appears to be violated in all experimental settings of interest.
justification: Theorem 4.1 relies on Assumption 1.2 of strong concavity, but the experiments use linear, Leontief, and CES utilities which violate this.

claim: The authors do not sufficiently justify that adding a small regularizer preserves equilibria or quantify its practical effect.
justification: They only cite a prior result to claim regularization preserves equilibria and do not analyze or empirically quantify its practical impact.

claim: The claim of O(1/ε^3) complexity lacks a precise specification of the problem class or assumptions under which that bound holds.
justification: The paper clearly states Assumption 1’s Lipschitz‐smoothness and strong concavity conditions under which the O(1/ε³) complexity guarantee is derived.

claim: Several prior works report better complexity dependencies than the claimed O(1/ε^3), but those references and comparisons are not discussed.
justification: The paper does not address whether there exist omitted prior works with better complexity, so the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted from the paper alone.

claim: The algorithmic approach is very similar to 'Exploitability minimization in games and beyond', which reduces the paper's algorithmic novelty.
justification: The paper explicitly distinguishes GAES from exploitability minimization, addressing its limitations and proposing a novel GAN formulation to overcome pseudo-game issues.

claim: The paper does not provide a detailed empirical or theoretical comparison with the 'Exploitability minimization' algorithm.
justification: The paper empirically benchmarks GAES against the exploitability descent algorithm in Section 5 with detailed performance comparisons.

claim: The suggestion that computing GNE is easier under a distribution over problem instances is asserted without sufficient justification.
justification: The paper provides theoretical polynomial‐time convergence and sample complexity bounds as well as empirical results supporting easier GNE computation over distributions.

claim: The authors do not clarify which variant of the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition or related assumptions their complexity result relies on.
justification: The paper’s convergence analysis never defines or references any specific Polyak-Łojasiewicz variant or related assumption, relying only on Lipschitz-smoothness and strong concavity assumptions.

claim: The relevance of Daskalakis et al. (2009) to the min-max optimization discussion in Footnote 4 is unclear and unexplained.
justification: Footnote 4 cites Daskalakis et al. 2009 without explaining its relevance to the min-max optimization discussion.

claim: The submission document uses the default title, indicating the manuscript title was not updated before submission.
justification: The document’s title ‘Generative Adversarial Equilibrium Solvers’ is specific and not a default placeholder, so the title was updated before submission.

claim: The references are inconsistent and include many older papers cited only in arXiv form without uniform citation formatting or URLs.
justification: References maintain consistent author–title–venue formatting and older works are cited by journal or conference, not solely as arXiv preprints.

claim: Observation 1 and the immediately following equations contain underfull equation formatting that needs correction.
justification: The paper provides no evidence regarding underfull equation formatting around Observation 1.

claim: The appendix contains many overfull equations that require proper formatting and layout fixes.
justification: The paper provides no information on appendix equation formatting or layout issues.

claim: It is unclear whether M and N are learned feature maps; the paper should visualize them to clarify what these maps look like.
justification: The paper explicitly states M and N are trainable spatial and temporal feature maps, so it is clear they are learned feature maps.

claim: The paper fails to explicitly acknowledge prior work that inspired the Hadamard product decomposition and should add the appropriate citations.
justification: Section 3.2 explicitly cites tensor decomposition works (33;58;59) as inspiration for using the Hadamard product decomposition.

claim: The main paper does not include a visualization of C, which hinders reader understanding and should be added to a figure.
justification: Figure 7 in the main paper visualizes the canonical spatial feature map C, so the claim is incorrect.

claim: The paper lacks visualizations of M and N; if they are learnable feature maps, the authors should provide visual examples or supplemental figures.
justification: The paper describes learnable feature maps M and N but does not include any visual examples or supplemental figures for them.

claim: The textual description of C is not properly incorporated into the main figures or text and should be included to improve reader comprehension.
justification: The paper explicitly defines and illustrates the Canonical Spatial Feature Map C in both the main text and Figure 4.

claim: The reported loss function improvement is only 0.15 dB, which is a modest improvement and should not be described as a major difference.
justification: The paper reports only a +0.15 dB PSNR gain for per-frame quality and explicitly describes this improvement as marginal rather than major.

claim: The paper does not provide a qualitative figure comparing results with and without the loss function to justify whether the 0.15 dB improvement is significant.
justification: Figure 7 provides qualitative ablation comparisons with and without the temporal consistency loss (L_temp), illustrating the visual impact corresponding to the 0.15 dB improvement.

claim: The wall-clock latency results do not break down how much runtime is due to DATUM versus the authors' optimizations.
justification: The paper reports a 10-minute total runtime including DATUM but provides no separate latency breakdown between DATUM and ConVRT optimizations.

claim: Without a latency breakdown, readers cannot estimate the expected overhead of adding the authors' module to a base ATM method.
justification: The paper reports only aggregate runtime for the full pipeline and omits module-level latency breakdown, preventing estimation of the module’s overhead.

claim: The paper does not compare HydraLoRA with LoRA at higher ranks (r=16 or r=32), which would be a fairer baseline.
justification: The paper’s Table 2 directly compares HydraLoRA (r=8) with LoRA at ranks r=16 and r=32.

claim: The reported improvements over LoRA are only incremental, indicating insufficient performance gains.
justification: HydraLoRA outperforms standard LoRA by multiple percentage points across diverse benchmarks, showing meaningful gains rather than merely incremental improvements.

claim: Using LoRA with r=8 is unfair because it uses only half the parameters compared to HydraLoRA finetuning.
justification: The paper confirms LoRA (r=8) uses half the parameters of HydraLoRA but does not characterize this parameter difference as unfair.

claim: The evaluation lacks comparisons under equal inference latency or compute budget, which may bias the reported results.
justification: The paper reports fine-tuning energy and latency but provides no inference latency or compute-budget comparisons, confirming the evaluation lacks equal-budget inference benchmarks.

claim: The paper's claim that C-RLFT is superior to RLFT is supported only by results from the openchat-13b model.
justification: All C-RLFT performance comparisons against RLFT baselines are conducted solely on the openchat-13b model.

claim: Openchat-13b was distilled from GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, which themselves were trained using RL-based fine-tuning (RLFT).
justification: The paper uses GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 outputs as training data but does not state they were distilled or that GPT-4/3.5 were trained via RLFT.

claim: Because openchat-13b learned from models trained with RLFT, the experiments cannot demonstrate that C-RLFT outperforms RLFT directly.
justification: openchat-13b is fine-tuned from the base llama-2-13b without RLFT training, so it does not learn from RLFT models.

claim: The evidence only supports that C-RLFT outperforms supervised fine-tuning when distilling from GPT models, not that it outperforms RLFT.
justification: The paper shows openchat-13b with C-RLFT outperforms the SFT+RLFT baseline llama-2-chat-13b, demonstrating it beats RLFT, not just SFT.

claim: It is unclear whether the low-quality portion of the mixed dataset provides any benefit to model performance.
justification: Ablation studies demonstrate that incorporating sub-optimal GPT-3.5 data under C-RLFT improves model performance compared to using expert data alone.

claim: The paper lacks an ablation experiment training the LLaMA-based model solely on GPT-4 data to isolate the effect of low-quality data.
justification: Table 2 includes an ablation where the model is trained solely on GPT-4 data (only SFT, only GPT-4), contradicting the claim.

claim: The reviewer asks for reported performance when the model is trained only on GPT-4 data, indicating a missing comparison to evaluate low-quality data value.
justification: Paper includes experiments training on only GPT-4 data and does not mention any reviewer request for such comparison.

claim: The superiority claim depends on openchat-13b outperforming vicuna-13b-1.5, which may conflate distillation source quality with the proposed method's effect.
justification: The paper’s ablation shows openchat-13b outperforms both vicuna-13b-1.5 and GPT-4-only SFT models, isolating method effect from data quality.

claim: The experimental comparison is limited, primarily featuring methods from Tang et al., 2022, lacking other weakly supervised baselines.
justification: Experiments compare mostly to Tang et al. (2022) methods with only one LLP baseline, omitting broader weakly supervised baselines.

claim: The paper does not report fully supervised accuracies on the same train/test splits, which would enhance evaluation.
justification: The paper includes fully supervised baseline accuracies ("Supervised" rows) in its experimental tables using the same datasets and splits.

claim: The paper lacks a comprehensive study of the method's limitations regarding constraints on m (number of unlabeled sets) and n_i (number of data points per set).
justification: The paper includes extensive experiments varying both m and n_i, analyzing robustness and limitations.

claim: Theorem 3.5 lacks discussion of practical implications and connection to the actual classification task involving class labels.
justification: Theorem 3.5 provides only a theoretical generalization bound without addressing practical implications or explicitly connecting to actual class-label prediction tasks.

claim: The paper does not investigate the impact of small m and large variations in label proportions across sets on generalizability with respect to m and n_i.
justification: Experiments vary m (10–1000), n_i sizes, and label-prior distributions, assessing generalizability with respect to m and set sizes.

claim: The paper does not clarify the difference between its Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 1 of Lu et al., ICML 2021.
justification: The paper cites Lu et al. (2021) as binary predecessor but never explicitly contrasts Lemma 3.1 with that paper’s Theorem 1.

claim: The paper fails to outline constraints on m and n required for practical significance, given that small label proportion differences may necessitate a large m.
justification: The paper specifies the full column–rank requirement on m but provides no explicit finite-sample or n constraints for practical significance.

claim: The proposed approach performs significantly worse under certain settings, such as a random class prior matrix and non-constrained m.
justification: Experimental results show the proposed RCM and CCM methods consistently outperform baselines even with random class-prior matrices and varying numbers of unlabeled sets.

claim: The paper does not clearly state how test accuracies were computed.
justification: The paper explicitly describes computing mean test accuracy over the last ten epochs (and specific epoch for U-Stop) across multiple trials.

claim: The paper does not state whether test data were balanced across classes when reporting accuracies.
justification: The paper does not mention the class balance of any test datasets when reporting the accuracy results.

claim: The paper does not analyze whether class size variations in datasets influenced the reported performance differences.
justification: The paper contains no evaluation or discussion on how class size variations influence its performance results.

claim: The sentence conflating class priors with class labels introduces confusion, since data points are typically assumed independent conditioned on their class labels.
justification: The paper does not address conflating class priors with class labels or related confusion, so it is insufficient to confirm the claim.

claim: Label proportions and class priors are practically equivalent in this context, so there is no clear dependence-based difference between MCMU and LLP.
justification: The paper explicitly states data points are independent in MCMU but dependent in LLP, so label proportions and class priors are not equivalent.

claim: The paper should use the term 'label proportions' instead of 'class priors' within each set to avoid terminological confusion.
justification: The paper consistently uses “class priors” without discussing renaming to “label proportions,” so its support for that terminological change is undetermined.

claim: Section 4.1 incorrectly uses 'randomly generated' when it should say 'randomly sampled' because data is drawn from existing distributions.
justification: Section 4.1 explicitly states data are “randomly sampled,” not “randomly generated,” contradicting the claim.

claim: The related work section lacks an early explanation for why negative empirical risk occurs in prior methods, which would help readers anticipate those issues.
justification: Section 2.3 explicitly describes why negative empirical risk occurs, citing unbounded unbiased risk estimators in prior methods

claim: The paper uses the index i both for unlabeled sets and for data points, creating potential notational confusion for readers.
justification: The paper consistently uses i for unlabeled set indices and r or v for data‐point indices, avoiding any reuse of i for both purposes.

claim: Theorem 3.6 defines p(y=j|\bar{y},x) as the probability that x's ground-truth label is j, which is misleading; it should denote the probability x belongs to class j.
justification: Theorem 3.6 explicitly defines p(y=j|¯y,x) as the probability that x belongs to class j, i.e. that its true label equals j, matching the correct interpretation.

claim: Theorem 3.6 assumes p(x|y=j)=p(x|y=j,\bar{y}), but conditional distributions estimated from all class j data and from a single unlabeled set may differ in practice.
justification: The paper explicitly assumes p(x|y=j)=p(x|y=j,¯y) in Theorem 3.6 but does not address that practical estimates from individual unlabeled sets may differ.

claim: The paper lacks justification for the testing framework used for Python and Java functions in BioCoder, with no detailed description of its design or rationale.
justification: The paper provides extensive details on the design, rationale, and implementation of its Python and Java testing framework, including fuzz-testing syntax, Docker setup, and AWS orchestration.

claim: The process by which test cases are described as 'randomly generated' and inserted into context files is not explained in the main paper or appendices L and Y.
justification: Section 3.4 and Appendix L describe the custom syntax and mechanisms for random test case generation and insertion into context files.

claim: Appendix L only briefly outlines the testing pipeline and does not explain how the approach provides a 'secure and efficient testing framework' or guarantees evaluation robustness.
justification: Appendix L merely summarizes high‐level testing steps without detailing how security, efficiency, or robustness guarantees are actually implemented or ensured.

claim: For Rosalind functions, the authors do not explain why or how generated code outputs are compared with cached golden outputs, leaving the comparison procedure unclear.
justification: The paper explicitly states that golden outputs are cached ahead and generated code outputs are executed in context and compared against these cached golden outputs.

claim: The paper provides no experimental results or examples that illustrate the outcomes of comparing generated code outputs to golden outputs for Rosalind problems.
justification: The paper includes a dedicated Rosalind evaluation (Table 5) reporting Pass@K results comparing generated outputs against golden code.

claim: The implemented correction mechanisms for rectifying minor syntax and style errors are not defined, so it is unclear which errors are considered 'minor' and harmless to functionality.
justification: The paper mentions using unspecified “basic correction mechanisms” for minor syntax/style errors without defining which errors qualify as minor or detailing the mechanisms.

claim: Applying unspecified correction mechanisms may bias the reported error distribution, undermining the validity of treating syntax and runtime errors as major failure reasons.
justification: The paper describes applying correction mechanisms but does not analyze their impact on error statistics or comment on potential bias in syntax/runtime error distributions.

claim: Table 4’s prompt format explanations are relegated to Appendix I, making the table hard to interpret in isolation within the main paper.
justification: The paper states that detailed prompt explanations for Table 4 are provided in Appendix I, indicating they are not included in the main text.

claim: Appendix I gives prompt examples but lacks high-level guidelines explaining how the five prompt versions were designed and what distinguishes their characteristics.
justification: Appendix I provides high-level descriptions of each of the five prompt versions and explains how they differ in design and characteristics.

claim: The paper claims an inverse relationship between prompt length and code generation performance without reconciling contradictory evidence from Table 4 showing shorter 'Necessary only' prompts often have lower pass rates.
justification: The paper explicitly notes that prompt length isn’t the sole driver of performance and discusses counterexamples from Table 4, contradicting the claim it ignored such evidence.

claim: The discussion of prompt effects is shallow and focuses on prompt length rather than analyzing prompt structure and content differences that may influence performance.
justification: The paper conducts an extensive analysis of multiple prompt styles and structural/content variations beyond mere length, contradicting the claim of a shallow, length-focused discussion.

claim: Appendix U’s 'Summary At Bottom' results appear incomplete because the table lacks a row for GPT-4, suggesting missing reported results.
justification: Appendix U’s Table 11 explicitly lists GPT-4 performance metrics under “Summary at Bottom,” refuting the claim of a missing GPT-4 row.

claim: Figure 3 is not clearly correlated with the described testing framework in section 3.4, and the reviewer suggests Figure 17 in Appendix R as a better example.
justification: The paper does not discuss any reviewer comment or link Figure 3 to Figure 17 suggestions, so insufficient evidence to confirm the claim.

claim: The paper does not state whether the five prompt styles were derived from prior literature, lectures, or experimental experience, leaving their provenance unspecified.
justification: The paper explicitly describes deriving prompt styles via careful experimentation, GPT-3.5-assisted summaries, and manual/context filtering processes.

claim: The paper does not justify why model editing is necessary given widespread use of APIs and their capabilities.
justification: The paper never discusses API usage or compares editing necessity against API capabilities, focusing instead on hardware constraints and resource budgets.

claim: The paper fails to specify who (which users or organizations) would be responsible for performing model editing in practice.
justification: The paper does not specify any users or organizations responsible for performing model editing in practice.

claim: The paper does not identify scenarios where model editing is preferable to fine-tuning or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches.
justification: The paper contains no comparison to fine-tuning or RAG nor any scenarios where editing is preferred, focusing exclusively on evaluating editing methods.

claim: The paper does not provide the algorithmic complexity in terms of input dimension, output dimension, batch size, and number of parameters.
justification: The paper only reports per-layer time/storage in terms of neuron counts h(l), not overall complexity by input/output dimension, batch size, or total parameter number.

claim: The paper does not analyze how the proposed method's computational cost scales with input dimension.
justification: The authors empirically measure forward Laplacian runtime and memory versus input dimension but do not provide a full asymptotic analysis of the KFAC method’s cost in d.

claim: The reviewer expects the method's computational cost to scale quadratically with the input dimension.
justification: The paper shows empirical and theoretical evidence that the computational cost of the forward Laplacian scales linearly rather than quadratically with input dimension.

claim: The forward Laplacian approach likely improves scaling only by a constant factor.
justification: The paper reports that the forward Laplacian framework yields about a twofold speedup and roughly half the memory usage, indicating only constant-factor scaling improvements.

claim: Prior work argued there may be no algorithm to compute the diagonal of the Hessian that is linear in dimension using automatic differentiation.
justification: The paper does not discuss any prior impossible algorithm claim for computing the Hessian diagonal in linear time with automatic differentiation.

claim: It remains unclear how general the KFAC weight-sharing approach is, for example how to apply it to higher-order PDEs or other neural network models.
justification: The paper explicitly generalizes the KFAC weight-sharing approach to arbitrary higher-order PDEs and network architectures, demonstrating its wide applicability.

claim: The paper omits critical details of the phylogenetic inference setup, specifically not specifying what the states are.
justification: The paper explicitly defines phylogenetic states as forests of singleton trees gradually joined by new nodes, so state definitions are provided.

claim: The paper omits critical details of the phylogenetic inference setup, specifically not specifying what the actions are.
justification: Section 4.4 explicitly states that actions involve picking two trees and joining their roots to a newly added node.

claim: The paper fails to mention the alternative approach of training a single GFlowNet with a stochastic reward as used in prior work.
justification: The paper references Pan et al. (2023c) on stochastic generative flow networks with stochastic rewards, so it does mention that alternative approach.

claim: The experimental validation is thin and does not provide comprehensive empirical support for the proposed method.
justification: The paper presents extensive experiments across four diverse tasks with clear baselines and metrics, demonstrating strong empirical support for the proposed method.

claim: The paper does not compare client training objectives, such as using TB versus CB, as experimental baselines.
justification: The paper’s Table 2 explicitly compares FC-GFlowNet when clients use CB versus TB objectives, demonstrating a direct comparison of client training objectives.

claim: The contrastive loss is incorrectly claimed as original despite equivalent variance-based formulations in prior literature.
justification: The paper explicitly cites Zhang et al. (2023a) as first proposing the equivalent variance-based objective, so it does not incorrectly claim the contrastive loss as original.

claim: The loss in section 3.3 is mathematically equivalent to optimizing the variance of log P_F(τ) - log R(x) - log P_B(τ | x).
justification: The contrastive balance loss L_CB is defined as E[(ξ(τ)−ξ(τ′))²], which equals twice Var[ξ], where ξ(τ)=log p_F(τ) − log R(x) − log p_B(τ|x).

claim: Prior works (Malkin et al. ICLR 2023, Zhang et al. ICLR 2023, Richter et al. NeurIPS 2020) already described similar variance-reduction losses or VarGrad methods.
justification: The paper cites Malkin et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2023a) using variance-based objectives derived from Richter et al.’s VarGrad method (2020).

claim: Observed differences between the contrastive loss (CL) and TB in Figure 6 may be due to learning rate choices rather than intrinsic algorithmic differences.
justification: The paper shows CB outperforms TB across learning rate settings (Figure 8), indicating performance differences arise from algorithmic factors rather than learning rate choices.

claim: The authors do not reference Figure 7 in the main text, which shows CB performing similarly to TB/DB on other domains.
justification: Figure 7 illustrates the phylogenetic generative process, not CB vs TB/DB performance, so the claim about it showing CB performance is incorrect.

claim: The proofs in section 3.3 appear to reduce in one line to existing TB training and TB gradient analysis theorems, making the current proofs redundant.
justification: Section 3.2 proofs directly invoke existing TB theorems (Malkin et al. 2022 Prop. 1) and TB gradient analysis, reducing to known results in one line.

claim: The current proofs in section 3.3 are obfuscated and should be simplified to their one-line reductions to existing results.
justification: The paper contains no Section 3.3 or discussion of simplifying its proofs to one‐line reductions.

claim: The bound in Theorem 2 may be practically unhelpful when models drop modes under reverse-KL objectives because the parameter alpha_n can become very small.
justification: The claim about reverse-KL mode dropping leading to small αₙ and a practically unhelpful bound is not discussed or supported by Theorem 2 or the paper’s content.

claim: The paper does not derive similar error bounds for divergences that are less sensitive to mode-dropping than the Jeffrey divergence.
justification: Theoretical analysis only provides Jeffrey divergence bounds and no analogous bounds are derived for other less mode-dropping divergences.

claim: The authors omitted showing all four relevant plots in the main text, which would better clarify when CB is helpful versus when it is not.
justification: The paper does not mention omitting four relevant plots in the main text or indicate that additional plots would clarify CB usefulness.

claim: The private-rewards application is unclear because sharing policies could allow recovering each client's reward density as the ratio of forward and backward policies.
justification: Lemma 1 shows that the ratio of forward and backward policies equals the client reward (up to normalization), implying shared policies leak each client’s reward density.

claim: It is unclear how the proposed phylogenetic inference experiments would scale to larger, realistic phylogenetic problems.
justification: The paper evaluates phylogenetic inference only on a small fixed‐leaf setting and provides no analysis or experiments on larger, realistic phylogenetic problems, leaving scalability unclear.

claim: The theoretical results assume linear neural networks and Gaussian-distributed weights, which are strong assumptions limiting applicability to realistic neural networks.
justification: The paper’s theory is developed for deep linear networks with Gaussian-initialized weights but then must transfer results empirically to realistic ReLU networks, indicating a restriction in applicability.

claim: The developed theoretical results do not produce a model that outperforms existing approaches, indicating limited practical improvement from the analysis.
justification: The paper’s theoretical insights guide design of wider networks achieving state-of-the-art certified accuracy, directly contradicting the claim of no practical improvement.

claim: The empirical evaluation is weak, relying on only a single MNIST model example for some claims.
justification: The paper presents extensive empirical studies across multiple datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, TinyImageNet) and architectures rather than relying on a single MNIST model.

claim: Only a few models and network configurations are evaluated, so the generality of the results across architectures and datasets is unclear.
justification: The paper empirically evaluates multiple architectures (varying depth and width) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, TinyImageNet), contradicting the claim of limited evaluation.

claim: Empirical observations on ReLU networks are presented, but it is unclear that these observations are consequences of the linear-theory developed.
justification: The paper shows theoretical transfer and empirical confirmation that ReLU results follow the developed linear-theory, so these observations are clearly consequences of that theory.

claim: The claim that certified training increases bound tightness is generic and is not convincingly attributed to the theoretical development in the paper.
justification: The paper provides Theorem 3.9 analytically proving IBP training increases tightness, contradicting the claim of unsubstantiated attribution.

claim: The claim that larger networks lead to better accuracy is generic and is not convincingly shown to follow from the proposed theory.
justification: The paper provides both theoretical and empirical results showing that increased network width yields improved certified accuracy.

claim: Figure 6 demonstrates width benefits only on a simple MNIST network, and larger networks and datasets are not evaluated.
justification: The paper evaluates width benefits on multiple architectures and datasets beyond MNIST, including CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet, contradicting the claim.

claim: The paper does not evaluate whether enlarging model size by four times yields measurable gains over state-of-the-art methods on modern models.
justification: The paper experimentally enlarges CNN width up to four times and demonstrates measurable gains in certified accuracy over state-of-the-art methods.

claim: The paper does not test whether observed gains are consistent across multiple architectures, training methods, and datasets like CIFAR and TinyImageNet.
justification: The paper empirically evaluates gains across several architectures (CNN3, CNN7, fully-connected), training methods (IBP, SABR, PGD, STAPS), and datasets including CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet.

claim: The authors do not explore reparameterizing networks to guarantee tight bounds and restrict training to a subspace of weights, as suggested by Theorem 3.4.
justification: The paper derives sign conditions for propagation invariance in Theorem 3.4 but does not propose reparameterizing networks or restricting training to that subspace of weights.

claim: State-of-the-art L2 certified defenses use reparameterization techniques, such as orthogonal convolution layers, which the paper does not discuss or compare against.
justification: The paper focuses on L∞ IBP-based certified training and does not mention or compare orthogonal convolution or other reparameterization techniques for L2 defenses.

claim: Results extended to a two-layer ReLU network are not emphasized or sufficiently highlighted in the paper's presentation.
justification: The paper includes but does not clearly emphasize two-layer ReLU extensions, so emphasis sufficiency is not determinable.

claim: The paper lacks explicit comparisons with modern certified training methods like CROWN-IBP, SABR, and MTL-IBP.
justification: The paper experimentally evaluates SABR and cites CROWN-IBP and MTL-IBP baselines, so it does include explicit comparisons with those methods.

claim: The paper's title overreaches by implying comprehensive coverage of training-free guidance beyond the specific subset of works actually addressed.
justification: The paper explicitly acknowledges that it does not encompass all training-free guidance approaches, contradicting the claim that the title overreaches by implying comprehensive coverage.

claim: The manuscript insufficiently articulates the rationale for focusing specifically on training-free approaches compared to other approaches.
justification: The paper clearly motivates training-free guidance by contrasting it with resource-intensive training-based methods and emphasizing plug-and-play use of off-the-shelf predictors without retraining.

claim: The theoretical underpinnings presented in the paper are not elaborated enough to fully substantiate the claimed theoretical grounding of the unified framework.
justification: The paper provides formal theorems and proofs (Theorem 3.2 and Lemma 3.3) elaborating its theoretical foundation and unifying existing methods.

claim: The authors' claim that training-free studies reduce to a hyperparameter study within their framework is unsupported because the framework's search space may omit important hyperparameters used in prior works.
justification: Theorem 3.2 explicitly shows all existing training-free methods are special cases in the TFG hyperparameter space, refuting the claim of omitted hyperparameters.

claim: Lemma 4.1 appears to restate an established MMSE variance formula widely used in prior diffusion literature, leaving unclear its novel contribution to the framework.
justification: The paper does not include or reference a Lemma 4.1, so its purported content and novelty cannot be assessed.

claim: There is no provided assurance that generated images produced by the method follow the intended conditional distribution as asserted in the paper.
justification: The paper offers no formal proof or unbiased sampling guarantee that its training-free method yields samples exactly from the target conditional distribution, relying instead on empirical evaluation.

claim: Equation (7) is presented without a guarantee or proof that the loss decreases at each iteration as the equation suggests.
justification: The paper presents the iterative update in Equation (7) without any accompanying theorem or proof guaranteeing that the loss decreases at each step.

claim: The concept of 'time-travel' being modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process lacks a detailed derivation or justification within the paper.
justification: The paper only briefly cites an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck interpretation of the recurrence strategy without providing any formal mathematical derivation or detailed justification.

claim: Key hyperparameter selection choices in the proposed method are not grounded in theory or given principled justification in the manuscript.
justification: The manuscript provides theoretical analyses (e.g. Lemma 3.3, Theorem 3.2) and principled empirical studies justifying each hyperparameter choice.

claim: The framework does not explicitly cover specific hyperparameter settings critical for existing works, such as the step size formula used in Face generation (at.sqrt()).
justification: The paper’s defined hyperparameter space (ρ, μ, γ, N_recur, N_iter) omits any mention of the at.sqrt() step-size formula used in face generation.

claim: The framework omits the specific hyperparameter formulation used in FreeDoM style transfer, namely the complex correction and norm_grad based scaling expression.
justification: Section E.4 explicitly states that the FreeDoM style transfer’s complex correction and gradient‐norm scaling schedule is omitted from the TFG framework.

claim: The hyperparameter search settings used for baseline methods in experimental comparisons are not disclosed, raising concerns about comparison fairness.
justification: The paper details baseline hyperparameter choices and search procedures in Section 5 and Appendix E (Table 11), contradicting the claim that they were undisclosed.

claim: When the forward model is known, generating many samples to train a conditional diffusion model is computationally cheap, making training-based approaches potentially superior to training-free approaches.
justification: The paper states training-based guidance requires resource-intensive specialized training, contradicting the claim that sample generation for training is computationally cheap.

claim: The paper does not explain how cited training-free works (e.g., [1]-[3]) relate to its scope or how they are encompassed by the proposed framework.
justification: The paper’s Section 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 explicitly show how existing training-free methods are encompassed within the proposed framework.

claim: Several techniques introduced in the paper are presented without direct theoretical underpinning or proofs linking them to the claimed performance gains.
justification: The paper provides theoretical analysis for some components (e.g., variance guidance lemma) but relies on empirical evidence rather than formal proofs for other techniques’ performance gains.

claim: The central assumption that ||w|| = ||\hat{w}|| + o(||w||) is contentious and may not hold in practical fixed-bit quantization scenarios.
justification: The paper assumes ∥ŵ∥=∥w∥+o(∥w∥) without discussing its practical validity in fixed-bit quantization, so there's insufficient evidence to confirm the claim.

claim: Under fixed-bit quantization, the difference between ||w|| and ||\hat{w}|| scales on the order of ||w||, contradicting the small o(||w||) assumption.
justification: The paper’s analysis of uniform scalar quantization in Appendix A.1 shows ∥w−ŵ∥=O(∥w∥) under fixed R, contradicting the o(∥w∥) assumption without growing R accordingly.

claim: Lemma 1 lacks a rigorous presentation, particularly regarding the o(·) notation and its formal justification.

claim: Equation 1 is insufficient because the paper fails to specify the underlying structural functions before presenting the causal graph.
justification: The paper explicitly defines the structural functions f_X_t and f_Y_t as bijective additive noise models, satisfying Equation 1 before presenting the causal graph.

claim: The work relies on intuitive causal graphs without formally defining structural functions, making the causal claims informal and unreliable.
justification: The paper explicitly defines structural functions via SCM equations and provides formal identifiability conditions, so its causal claims are not merely informal.

claim: Figure 1 lacks a concrete example mapping L_i, X, Y, and T to a specific task to clarify what each variable represents in practice.
justification: Figure 1 presents only the abstract causal graph without any concrete task example mapping of L_i, X, Y, and T.

claim: In Figure 1, representing Y_t as a single node is misleading; Y should be notated as distinct nodes for different tasks t.
justification: Figure 1 already depicts separate Y_t nodes for each task t with distinct subscripts, contradicting the claim that they are represented as a single node.

claim: If the task variable T is observed during task execution, it cannot plausibly act as a backdoor confounder producing spurious correlations as claimed.
justification: In the meta-SCM, T is observed and has no causal edges that create backdoor paths, so it cannot act as a confounder.

claim: The conditional independence L_i ⟂ L_j | T in Figure 1 appears to contradict the paper's claim that non-causal latent factors correlate with Y_t via T.
justification: The paper does not posit any conditional independence L_i ⟂ L_j | T, nor discuss non-causal factor correlations via T, so the claim cannot be verified.

claim: The authors do not provide a specific concrete example (for instance, a simple text classification) showing how non-causal factors become correlated with Y_t.
justification: The paper discusses spurious correlations abstractly but provides no concrete text classification example illustrating non-causal factors correlating with Y_t.

claim: The paper fails to explain how standard training procedures cause models to learn spurious correlations arising from the task confounder T.
justification: The paper explicitly explains that existing methods exploit spurious correlations due to inherent dataset properties D affecting latent factors, causing non‐causal features to influence predictions.

claim: Assuming the only confounder is the task variable T appears unrealistic, and the paper does not justify the applicability of this assumption to real tasks.
justification: The paper posits task variable T as the sole confounder without empirical analysis or theoretical justification for its realism or applicability to real-world tasks.

claim: Section 3.2 is unclear about whether the method alleviates spurious correlations via backdoor adjustment, intervened data, or another mechanism.
justification: Section 3.2 exclusively develops identifiability theory and does not describe whether spurious correlations are alleviated by backdoor adjustment, intervened data, or any other mechanism.

claim: The paper's definition of identifiability is confusing and does not clearly state what object or quantity is meant to be identifiable.
justification: The paper explicitly defines identifiability of the latent factors via Definition 1, clarifying what is to be identified.

claim: Identifiability is typically defined for specific causal quantities between variables rather than for an entire SCM, but the paper treats identifiability at the SCM level without justification.
justification: The paper provides theoretical Uniform Identifiability Conditions with formal proofs demonstrating identifiability at the SCM level, directly contradicting the claim of lacking justification.

claim: The causal quantity that the proposed UIC loss in Equation 6 is intended to measure is vague and left unspecified.
justification: The paper clearly defines the UIC loss in Equation 6 as enforcing distinct child-set adjacency (via a differentiable indicator on matrix A), so it is specified.

claim: The paper does not justify why identifiable latent factors would necessarily correspond to the true causal factors of Y_t.
justification: The paper proves latent factor identifiability but does not explain why those identifiable factors correspond to the true causal factors for Y_t.

claim: The paper does not convincingly demonstrate or theoretically justify that the UIC loss can reliably select identifiable factors from the latent representation.
justification: The paper proposes UIC and adds it as a loss term but does not provide a formal proof that the UIC loss reliably recovers the identifiable latent factors.

claim: The experimental evaluation compares only against two simple baselines, which may not be sufficiently advanced to validate the proposed method's performance.
justification: The paper only compares the proposed method against two baselines (MFT and Vanilla-IT), without evaluating more advanced methods to further validate performance.

claim: The paper overlooks several crucial references relevant to active learning, including works that explore the theoretical importance of near decision boundaries.
justification: The paper’s content provides no information on whether it omitted those theoretical works on decision boundaries, leaving the claim unverified.

claim: Key foundational concepts in the paper echo pre-existing active learning methodologies that are not appropriately credited.
justification: The paper explicitly cites and discusses key prior active learning methods demonstrating appropriate credit for foundational concepts.

claim: The claimed linear-time scalable algorithm replicates ideas previously introduced in prior work [3] and is not acknowledged as such.
justification: The paper explicitly cites and contrasts prior probability-based diversity methods like CDAL (Agarwal et al., 2020), so it does not fail to acknowledge such ideas.

claim: A prior approach like PowerBALD or PowerEntropy uses sampling similar to the paper's Eq (6) and proposes more original scaling maintaining linear-time complexity.
justification: The paper does not mention PowerBALD or PowerEntropy, so no evidence confirms or denies that such methods use Eq (6) style sampling and linear-time scaling.

claim: The active learning results for LeNet on EMNIST or RepeatedMNIST seem unconvincing compared to literature that achieves comparable accuracy with 300–500 labeled images.
justification: The paper does not reference or evaluate literature claiming comparable accuracy on EMNIST or RepeatedMNIST with only 300–500 labeled images.

claim: The paper reports needing more than 1000 labeled images to match supervised accuracy, which deviates from established benchmarks requiring around 300–500 images.
justification: The paper does not report or compare needing over 1000 labeled images nor reference benchmarks of 300–500 images to match supervised accuracy.

claim: The LeNet experimental setup and implementation details are insufficiently described and should be revisited to validate the reported results.
justification: The paper only states using LeNet for 20 epochs without specifying optimizer, learning rate, batch size, or architecture details, indicating insufficient experimental description.

claim: BADGE performance appears suboptimal in the paper, suggesting hyperparameters were not adequately tuned for a fair comparison.
justification: The paper does not discuss BADGE hyperparameter tuning or claim its performance was suboptimal due to inadequate tuning.

claim: The paper does not provide explicit explanation of how diversity is sourced or incorporated in the proposed formula, limiting interpretability and generalizability.
justification: The paper explicitly defines diversity through probability-space distances, initial margin uncertainty, update equations, and integrates it in the relevance score, contradicting the claim.

claim: The margin-based measure considers two class boundaries and may not generalize to multiclass settings without further justification.
justification: The paper defines and justifies margin uncertainty explicitly for C-class classification, demonstrating its use and generalization in multiclass settings without additional assumptions.

claim: Experimental evaluation is limited and omits more challenging benchmarks such as CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet.
justification: Paper evaluates only on MNIST variants, SVHN, medical and tabular data, omitting CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet.

claim: Section 4.4 indicates different benchmarks require distinct gamma values but the paper provides no guidance for choosing gamma a priori.
justification: Section 4.4 recommends a default γ=10 and notes performance is stable for γ in [5,20], providing clear a priori guidance for choosing γ.

claim: The presentation lacks explicit acknowledgment of prior works [1], [2], [3], and [4], which undermines the paper's originality claim.
justification: The paper explicitly cites and contrasts numerous prior works throughout its introduction and related work sections, contradicting the claim of missing acknowledgments.

claim: Experimental results, particularly for LeNet and BADGE, are inconclusive and require further rigor and validation to strengthen the paper's credibility.
justification: The paper provides extensive conclusive experiments showing strong performance for LeNet and BADGE, contradicting the claim of inconclusiveness.

claim: The paper lacks results on real-world X-ray/CT datasets such as DGKr and w7Ci, which are necessary to demonstrate real-world applicability.
justification: The paper evaluates only on synthetic and FIPS real-world datasets and does not report any results on DGKr or w7Ci datasets.

claim: The manuscript insufficiently discusses and references existing XR-GS works, reducing contextualization of the proposed approach for readers.
justification: The paper explicitly cites and analyzes existing XR-GS methods ([7], [14], [29]) in its related work, demonstrating sufficient discussion and contextualization.

claim: The authors do not explicitly state that their alpha-blending and per-Gaussian integration claims rely on the isotropic approximation of X-ray physics.
justification: The paper explicitly assumes isotropic X-ray density (σ is isotropic) and states anisotropic effects are ignored as noise, so reliance on isotropy is clearly declared.

claim: Claims that alpha-blending contradicts the unordered nature of X-ray imaging are only valid under the isotropic simplification and are not generally true.
justification: The paper does not address the general validity of alpha-blending claims beyond the isotropic density assumption.

claim: When physics effects like Compton scattering are considered, the ordering of Gaussians becomes important, which undermines the paper's unordered rasterization assumptions.
justification: The paper acknowledges Compton scattering as noise but does not analyze its impact on Gaussian ordering or unordered rasterization.

claim: The paper does not clearly compare the proposed GS voxelizer to existing CUDA-based differentiable solutions such as PyTorch3D's point-cloud-to-voxel implementation.
justification: The paper introduces its CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer but does not discuss or evaluate it against PyTorch3D or other existing CUDA differentiable voxelization implementations.

claim: It is unclear whether PyTorch3D's PC-to-voxel requires only minor tweaks to support Gaussians, so the claimed benefits of the proposed GS voxelizer are not justified.
justification: The paper does not discuss PyTorch3D’s PC-to-voxel or compare it, so it is unclear whether minor tweaks could achieve similar voxelization benefits.

claim: The authors should include the additional real-world experiments reported in their rebuttal (rebuttal Tab.1 and Fig.1) within the main manuscript.
justification: The paper does not mention any rebuttal experiments or discuss including additional real-world results.

claim: The manuscript omits discussed references such as the cited TV reference [c], which should be included for completeness and proper attribution.
justification: The manuscript provides no information regarding a cited TV reference [c], so its omission cannot be confirmed or denied.

claim: The paper fails to cite or discuss recent preprints (e.g., DDGS-CT and Unified Gaussian Primitives) that address ordering and scattering simulation relevant to XR-GS.
justification: The paper cites DDGS-CT but does not mention Unified Gaussian Primitives, so it only partially omits recent related preprints.

claim: The proposed model is not sufficiently novel because combining local and global perspectives in graph models is already a common idea.
justification: The paper explicitly claims to be the first temporal graph model to jointly integrate both global and local perspectives, contradicting the claim that this fusion is already common.

claim: The paper lacks a detailed discussion of temporal point process approaches and their relevance to the proposed temporal graph method.
justification: The paper contains no section or detailed discussion on temporal point process methods or their relevance to the proposed approach.

claim: The paper does not provide experimental comparisons with temporal point process-based temporal graph models such as Lu et al. (2019) and WWW 2022.
justification: The paper’s baselines exclude the Lu et al. (2019) and any WWW 2022 temporal point process models, so no experimental comparisons with those methods are provided.

claim: The motivation sentence about pairwise interactions having different temporal properties is not clearly explained or connected to the proposed method.
justification: The paper explicitly links differing temporal properties to its global TCN module and local time-weighted aggregation, directly connecting the motivation to the GLEN method.

claim: The sentence regarding endogenous and exogenous factors driving the generative process is not clearly connected to or motivating the proposed methodology.
justification: The paper explicitly cites endogenous and exogenous factor complexity to motivate combining global and local perspectives in its proposed method.

claim: In Table 2, the Random strategy outperforms historical and inductive strategies, which is surprising and lacks sufficient discussion.
justification: Table 2 shows random sampling outperforms other strategies, but the paper discusses performance drops under historical and inductive sampling.

claim: There is a discrepancy between the UCI results reported in Table 2 and Table 3, indicating inconsistent or unreliable experimental reporting.
justification: UCI AP for GLEN under Random sampling differs between Table 2 (99.11) and Table 3 (98.47), confirming a reporting discrepancy.

claim: The paper should include additional experimental comparisons with temporal point process methods to validate claimed advantages of GLEN over global modeling approaches.
justification: The paper does not discuss or propose adding further temporal point process comparisons to validate GLEN’s advantages over global modeling approaches.

claim: The decision to frame the learning task as a POMDP lacks clear justification in the manuscript.
justification: The paper explicitly justifies using a POMDP by modeling learners with limited sensory capacities requiring belief updates under partial observability.

claim: The paper provides insufficient concrete examples to justify framing the teaching problem as a POMDP.
justification: The paper presents detailed toy and gridworld environments formalized as POMDPs with states, actions, observations, and belief updates, contradicting the claim of insufficient examples.

claim: The manuscript does not clearly present the task formulation for the Theory-of-Mind (ToM) teacher.
justification: Section 3.3 explicitly formulates the ToM-teacher’s task as a contextual multi-armed bandit with utility definition and Bayesian inference.

claim: The paper fails to clearly differentiate its approach from prior POMDP-like teaching works, leaving technical novelty unclear.
justification: The related work section explicitly contrasts POMDP-based and ToM methods, clearly detailing how this approach differs and its novel contributions.

claim: The paper's primary objective is vaguely defined, making the core contribution and takeaway unclear.
justification: The paper explicitly states its objectives in the abstract and introduction, clearly defining its core contribution and takeaway.

claim: It is unclear whether the main claim is that Bayesian ToM-teachers better capture human internal state changes.
justification: The paper explicitly claims improved teaching efficiency, not better capturing human internal state changes.

claim: During testing, the student's actions are driven by a basic decision tree, implying minimal uncertainty in learner behavior.
justification: Learner actions follow a decision-tree policy, but the paper models substantial uncertainty through Bayesian belief updates.

claim: The empirical evaluation lacks human-subject experiments to validate real-world impact.
justification: The paper’s experiments are solely in simulated environments with artificial agents and include no human-subject studies to assess real-world impact.

claim: Equation 3 and related discussion suggest the teaching policy is essentially greedy.
justification: Equation 3 explicitly defines the teacher’s one-step utility maximization for selecting demonstrations, i.e. a greedy policy.

claim: A greedy teaching policy may be suboptimal over time and is not justified without a well-defined teaching task.
justification: The paper shows that non-adaptive greedy teaching policies (e.g. maximizing reward only) achieve significantly lower utility than utility-based adaptive teachers with a well-defined teaching task.

claim: The manuscript omits important related works and lacks proper positioning within existing literature.
justification: The paper’s Section 2 reviews diverse human pedagogy, ToM, machine teaching, and Bayesian inference works, demonstrating proper literature positioning.

claim: The paper does not include comparisons with prior methods such as Srivastava et al. and Yu et al.
justification: The paper cites Srivastava et al. and Yu et al. in related work but presents no experimental or theoretical comparisons to those prior methods.

claim: The authors assume the teacher has a general idea of the student's policy, but the realism of this assumption is not justified.
justification: The paper explicitly assumes the teacher has access to an approximate learner policy without providing any empirical or theoretical justification for the realism of this assumption.

claim: The paper claims to estimate learner transition and observation parameters but does not clearly explain how the learner's internal goal is estimated.
justification: The paper explicitly describes Bayesian inference (Equation 4) for updating beliefs over learner goals, thus clearly explaining how the internal goal is estimated.

claim: The evaluation setup may minimize learner behavior uncertainty, limiting the evaluation's realism and generalizability.
justification: The paper does not assess whether its evaluation setup minimizes learner behavior uncertainty or affects realism and generalizability.

claim: The paper does not discuss alternative label integration methods for crowdsourcing nor clarify that no such alternatives exist.
justification: The Related Work section reviews multiple alternative crowdsourcing label integration methods, contradicting the claim.

claim: The paper lacks motivation and justification for choosing a KNN-based method over other established label integration approaches reported in prior surveys.
justification: The paper clearly motivates leveraging neighbor instances and justifies an adaptive KNN approach over fixed-K label integration methods cited in prior work.

claim: Some specific claims (Q4) in the paper are not experimentally verified and require empirical evaluation to be supported.
justification: The paper contains no mention of any specific "Q4" claims or their experimental verification, so their status cannot be determined.

claim: The paper fails to clearly define which type(s) of crowdsourcing tasks the proposed method targets.
justification: The paper explicitly addresses classification crowdsourcing tasks (binary and multi-class label integration).

claim: The proposed method may be applicable only to a limited set of task types, but the paper does not clarify these limitations.
justification: The paper does not discuss or clarify any task type limitations for its proposed method.

claim: The paper's title and certain content risk over-claiming general applicability without refining scope based on task limitations.
justification: The paper explicitly scopes KFNN to crowdsourcing label integration and discusses its limitations, avoiding any over-claim of general applicability.

claim: Experimental results show the proposed method performs worse than selected baselines on some datasets in Macro-F1 and integration accuracy by large margins.
justification: Tables 1 and 2 show KFNN underperforms certain baselines (e.g., MNLDP on anneal, MV on breast-cancer) by margins exceeding 5–10 points in Macro-F1 and accuracy.

claim: The evaluation indicates the proposed method is not consistently the optimal choice across the compared methods.
justification: Average integration accuracy shows LAWMV and MNLDP outperform KFNN, so KFNN is not consistently optimal across all compared methods.

claim: The proposed method has not been evaluated on real-world crowdsourcing platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk or CrowdFlower.
justification: The paper evaluates KFNN on two real-world datasets collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk.

claim: Current simulated experiments do not establish whether the proposed method can be effectively integrated and perform well in complex real-world crowdsourcing scenarios.
justification: Paper includes real-world experiments showing KFNN’s effectiveness on real-world datasets, contradicting the claim that experiments didn’t establish real-world performance.

claim: The evaluation lacks real-world double-blind testing commonly used in crowdsourcing studies to validate performance under realistic conditions.
justification: The paper’s evaluations use existing simulated and real-world datasets without any mention of real-world double-blind testing procedures.

claim: The paper does not compare its method against other label integration options identified in the seminal survey referenced by the reviewer.
justification: The paper evaluates KFNN against six state-of-the-art label integration algorithms from the referenced survey, demonstrating comparative experimental results.

claim: The method requires additional meta-training, increasing training complexity and resource demands.
justification: Paper defines a bi-level meta-training algorithm (Algorithm 2) adding an inner meta-update step that increases training complexity and resource demands.

claim: The paper lacks reported time costs for meta-learning training and for model inference, preventing assessment of computational efficiency.
justification: The paper includes training and inference time cost results (Tables 12 and 13) and time complexity analysis in Appendix B.11, contradicting the claim.

claim: The Chebyshev approximation used to avoid eigen-decomposition appears more computationally expensive than graph-structure-based approaches.
justification: The paper does not compare the computational cost of the Chebyshev approximation to graph‐structure‐based methods.

claim: The model seems difficult to apply to large graphs such as ogbn datasets due to computational expense and scalability concerns.
justification: The paper demonstrates successful application on large OGBN-Arxiv and OGBN-Products datasets, showing the model scales rather than being difficult to apply.

claim: The evaluation omits large-node-count graph datasets like ogbn, limiting evidence of scalability and generalization to large graphs.
justification: The paper explicitly reports experiments on large-node-count OGBN-arxiv and OGBN-product datasets, demonstrating scalability and generalization to large graphs.

claim: The reported performance is not close to state-of-the-art; more recent studies (e.g., cited [1], [2]) show better performance.
justification: The paper’s extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, contradicting the claim of underperformance.

claim: The paper lacks a detailed introduction to meta-learning, hindering readers' understanding of the experimental setup and method rationale.
justification: The paper only briefly introduces meta-learning in Section 4.3 without a dedicated detailed overview, which may hinder understanding of the experimental setup and rationale.

claim: The SparklesDialogueVG subset was generated using GPT-4, introducing dependency on the same model being evaluated.
justification: The paper confirms SparklesDialogueVG was generated using GPT-4, but it does not state that this creates dependency on the same model being evaluated.

claim: The paper compares model performance to GPT-4 despite GPT-4 being used to generate part of the training dataset.
justification: The paper uses GPT-4 to generate part of its training dataset (SparklesDialogue) and directly compares SparklesChat’s performance to GPT-4 in SparklesEval.

claim: SparklesChat performs worse than GPT-4 despite using much richer image embeddings.
justification: The paper reports GPT-4 scoring 9.26 versus SparklesChat’s 8.56 on SparklesEval despite SparklesChat using richer image embeddings.

claim: The paper presents no novel model architecture, with the primary contribution being the dataset rather than methodological innovation.
justification: SparklesChat reuses MiniGPT-4 architecture with only input interleaving changes, while main contributions are the SparklesDialogue dataset and SparklesEval benchmark.

claim: The dataset contains only two dialogue turns per sample, which limits modeling of longer conversational sessions.
justification: SparklesDialogue is explicitly generated with only two turns per dialogue, preventing training on longer conversational sessions.

claim: Limiting samples to only two turns sacrifices longer-session practicality in favor of more images per turn.
justification: The paper does not discuss trade-offs of using only two dialogue turns versus longer sessions for more images per turn.

claim: The dataset is machine-generated rather than human-created, weakening its value as the paper's principal contribution.
justification: The paper explicitly states SparklesDialogue is machine-generated and portrays it as a strength rather than weakening its principal contribution.

claim: Results are reported only for MiniGPT-4 extensions, lacking experiments that evaluate applicability to other approaches like LLaVA.
justification: The paper includes experiments on LLaVA-v1.5 models as well as MiniGPT-4, contradicting the claim that only MiniGPT-4 extensions were evaluated.

claim: The experiments section is weak and does not convincingly demonstrate the claimed improvements across diverse settings.
justification: The paper reports strong quantitative results on BISON, NLVR2, SparklesEval, and ablation studies, convincingly demonstrating improvements across diverse benchmarks.

claim: The overall contributions of the paper are weak, relying primarily on dataset creation rather than substantial technical advances.
justification: The paper does not address the subjective weakness of its contributions, focusing on presenting both a model innovation and new datasets rather than evaluating contribution strength.

claim: SparklesDialogueVG and SparklesEval use the same image and caption sources, creating potential overlap between training and evaluation sets.
justification: The paper states SparklesDialogueVG and SparklesEval both use Visual Genome images with SVIT captions, explicitly acknowledging shared sources and possible overlap.

claim: Shared sources between SparklesDialogueVG and SparklesEval may explain why the VG-trained model outperforms the CC-trained model.
justification: The paper explicitly notes that SparklesDialogueVG and SparklesEval share the same image sources, which partially explains VG-trained models’ stronger performance.

claim: Claiming SparklesDialogueVG as a high-quality subset is questionable given its potential overlap with the evaluation set.
justification: SparklesDialogueVG and SparklesEval share VG image sources, which the paper acknowledges could partially explain higher evaluation performance.

claim: Table 2 contains a typographical error: the column title under 'Turn two' should be labeled 'A2'.
justification: Table 2 already labels the first subcolumn under “Turn two” as “A2,” so there is no typographical error.

claim: The authors used a 95:5 train-test split on the MD22 dataset, making their results incomparable to baseline models that used different predefined splits.
justification: The paper states the authors used the same 95:5 train–test split and baseline train/validation splits as prior MD22 evaluations, ensuring direct comparability with baselines.

claim: The 95:5 split was applied to train-test in this work rather than to train-validation as in prior studies, causing inconsistent dataset partitioning.
justification: The paper applies a 95:5 split as a train-test split on the MD22 dataset, while prior studies’ 95:5 usage on train-validation splits is not detailed.

claim: Authors trained EGAP on the entire MD22 dataset while baseline models reserved substantial test sets, effectively reducing the authors' test set size.
justification: The authors used a 95:5 train-test split on MD22 matching baseline splits, not training on the entire dataset.

claim: The authors used a different train/validation/test partitioning than baseline models instead of only adding extra training data, invalidating direct performance comparisons.
justification: The paper does not specify using different train/validation/test splits from the baseline models, so the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: The authors assert that performance saturates quickly with dataset size but provide no experimental evidence or analyses to support this claim.
justification: The paper includes an ablation study (Figure 6) showing performance trends across varying dataset sizes, contradicting the assertion of no supporting evidence.

claim: Experiments on OC20 were performed only on the 2M S2EF split instead of larger S2EF-All or S2EF-All+MD splits, weakening scalability and efficiency claims.
justification: The paper reports experiments on both OC20 2M and All+MD splits, contradicting the claim that only the 2M split was used.

claim: On the OC20 2M split, EGAP underperforms on force metrics while outperforming on energy metrics, making the reported performance advantage inconclusive.
justification: Paper shows EScAIP outperforms baselines on both energy and force metrics on the OC20 2M split.

claim: Because training trades off energy and force predictions, prioritizing one metric can explain observed differences, so metric differences do not demonstrate overall superiority.
justification: The paper does not discuss any trade-off between energy and force metrics or imply that metric prioritization invalidates claims of overall superiority.

claim: The authors did not provide experiments varying model size or parameter count, so their scalability claims lack empirical support.
justification: The paper presents ablation studies and small/medium/large EScAIP models varying parameter counts with clear performance scaling evidence.

claim: The paper reports baseline results for VisNet-LSRM Tetrasaccharide that do not match values in Li et al. (2024), indicating numerical discrepancies.
justification: Table 6 shows VisNet-LSRM Tetrasaccharide energies of 0.044 vs 0.053 from the original Li et al. (2024), confirming numerical discrepancies.

claim: Discrepancies between the authors' reported baseline numbers and the original papers raise concerns about the accuracy and fairness of the reported comparisons.
justification: The paper does not discuss discrepancies between reported baseline numbers and original papers or fairness concerns in reported comparisons.

claim: The authors' interpretation of SDA [1] is incorrect and misrepresents how SDA constructs intermediate posteriors and uses likelihood functions.
justification: The paper does not provide evidence to confirm or refute that their discussion misrepresents SDA’s intermediate posteriors or likelihood use.

claim: The approximated likelihood \hat{p}(y|x_t) should be treated as a likelihood function that defines a series of intermediate posteriors \hat{p}(x_t|y) across diffusion timesteps.
justification: The paper explicitly defines a sequence of intermediate posteriors using approximated timestep likelihoods as potentials to twist the diffusion prior across timesteps.

claim: The DDIM predictor approximates the transition from \hat{p}(x_t|y) to \hat{p}(x_{t-\Delta}|y), while the C Langevin corrector steps aim to produce samples from the resulting posterior.
justification: The paper does not describe a DDIM predictor approximating transitions nor C Langevin corrector steps as stated, making the claim unresolved by its content.

claim: DCPS and SDA sampling algorithms are similar in that both employ Langevin correction steps to reduce transition errors during sampling.
justification: Both DCPS and SDA explicitly include Langevin Monte Carlo correction steps to mitigate transition approximation errors during their sampling procedures.

claim: The manuscript does not discuss the substantive similarities between DCPS and SDA, particularly both methods' use of Langevin steps to correct transition errors.
justification: The paper’s Related Works section explicitly discusses SDA’s use of Langevin steps and compares these to DCPS’s Langevin corrections.

claim: DCPS defines the likelihood g^l_m(x_m) as the conditional expectation E[g_{k_l}(x_{k_l}) | x_m], rather than the rough approximation to E[g_0(x_0) | x_m] used in SDA.
justification: The paper indeed defines g^{ℓ,⋆}_m(x_m) via g^{ℓ,⋆}_m(x_m)=∫g_{k_ℓ}(x_{k_ℓ})p_{k_ℓ|m}(x_{k_ℓ}|x_m)dx_{k_ℓ}, i.e. E[g_{k_ℓ}(X_{k_ℓ})|X_m=x_m].

claim: The DCPS predictor spans multiple diffusion steps and uses a sequence of variational Gaussian approximations, which is substantially different from a single-step DDIM predictor.
justification: DCPS uses multiple diffusion‐step blocks with sequential variational Gaussian approximations, contrasting the single‐step DDIM predictor approach.

claim: Poorly chosen potentials g^l_m(x) can lead to unstable sampling behavior and degrade the method's robustness.
justification: The paper states that algorithm effectiveness and robustness rely on well-designed intermediate potentials and poor choices can impair performance.

claim: The reviewer believes that most observed quality gains in DCPS are attributable to the Langevin corrector steps rather than to the specific design of the potentials g^l_m(x).
justification: The paper does not isolate or evaluate whether quality gains arise chiefly from Langevin corrector steps versus the design of the potentials.

claim: Potentials defined as in Eq.(3.9)-(3.11) but using index m instead of k_l would likely perform nearly as well, suggesting the potential choice may not be the critical factor.
justification: The paper does not evaluate using Eq.(3.9)–(3.11) potentials indexed by m instead of k_ℓ, so evidence is insufficient to confirm or refute this claim.

claim: The authors misuse the term 'generation-time strategy', which typically refers to decoding methods like beam search or top-k sampling.
justification: The paper does not mention or define the term "generation-time strategy", so misuse cannot be assessed based on its content.

claim: The results presented in Table 5 do not support the paper's claim about a 'generation-time strategy'.
justification: Table 5 shows generation‐time strategies yield smaller win‐rate gains compared to NEFT, thus supporting rather than refuting the paper’s claim about generation‐time methods.

claim: Table 6 fails to report standard deviations for the experiments, preventing assessment of result reliability in low-resource settings.
justification: Table 6 presents only mean win rates and output lengths without any standard deviations, so reliability assessment is indeed prevented.

claim: The paper reports stable performance across changed noise statistics, which is counterintuitive because excessive noise should eventually degrade model performance.
justification: The paper presents ablations over uniform and Gaussian noise at multiple scales showing largely unchanged performance until extreme values, confirming stable performance across noise statistics.

claim: The authors provide only a vague statement that AlpacaEval's standard error is less than 2% without reporting the actual numeric values across experiments.
justification: The paper tables report precise AlpacaEval standard errors (e.g. ±0.40, ±0.52), not merely a vague statement without numeric values.

claim: The manuscript does not explain why NEFTune improves performance, lacking a mechanistic or theoretical justification of the method.
justification: The paper provides only empirical analyses and a hypothesis on reduced overfitting, explicitly stating it lacks a conclusive theoretical mechanism for NEFTune’s effectiveness.

claim: NEFTune injects uncontrolled noise into embedding representations, reducing interpretability of why performance improves.
justification: The paper adds tunable, uniformly sampled noise with a defined scale and analyzes performance improvements, rather than injecting uncontrolled noise or reducing interpretability.

claim: The authors do not analyze which noise statistics improve performance nor identify conditions where added noise will deteriorate results.
justification: The paper ablates noise type and scale, comparing uniform versus Gaussian noise and varying α values, thus identifying when noise improves or degrades performance.

claim: The paper lacks a baseline that represents each embedding as a cosine-similarity-weighted linear combination of related embeddings, as used in prior work.
justification: The paper’s experiments only compare standard finetuning and noise-based methods, with no baseline using cosine-similarity-weighted embedding combinations.

claim: The authors did not include a detailed comparison with earlier related methods such as bi-level finetuning with task-dependent similarity structure.
justification: The paper includes no discussion or detailed comparison of bi-level finetuning with task-dependent similarity structure in either related work or experiments.

claim: The authors did not test the suggested similarity-initialized embedding combination baseline, which might match or outperform NEFTune according to prior observations.
justification: The paper does not mention or evaluate any similarity-initialized embedding combination baseline, confirming the authors did not test it.
